tier_reason: The README tables come from the well-known third-party TurboBench harness (FPC is an integrated TurboBench codec) and show fpc 32 decoding silesia.tar at 897.28 MB/s versus 715.36 for fsehuf and 243.08 for zlibh on a Core i5-4460. A WebSearch snippet of powturbo's own Entropy Coder Benchmark (sites.google.com/site/powturbo/entropy-coder, blocked here) shows FPC 32 at 928.53 MB/s decode versus FSEhuf 32 at 831.45 MB/s, an independent run consistent with the claim. No compiler or flags are stated, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: silesia.tar (Core i5-4460, TurboBench): fpc 32 decodes at 897.28 MB/s versus 715.36 MB/s for fsehuf, 591.30 MB/s for rans_static16, 483.55 MB/s for fse and 243.08 MB/s for zlibh (about 1.25x fsehuf and 3.7x zlibh, derived from page data); fpc 16 compresses at 476.96 MB/s versus 248.55 MB/s for zlibh and decodes at 821.30 MB/s. Ratios are within 0.1 percentage points (61.4% for fpc 32 and fsehuf). On the Allwinner H3 board, enwik8: fpc 32 decodes at 90.70 MB/s versus 61.11 MB/s for fsehuf and 62.90 MB/s for zlibh. Independent powturbo Entropy Coder Benchmark (snippet only, file and CPU not seen): FPC 32 decode 928.53 MB/s versus FSEhuf 32 at 831.45 MB/s.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the benchmark run; the standalone Makefile uses -Wall -O2 -std=c99 -DNDEBUG
corrections.caveats: The README tables were run by the project author through the TurboBench harness; no compiler or flags stated for that run (the standalone Makefile uses -O2). The independent powturbo Entropy Coder Benchmark figure is from a WebSearch snippet only, since sites.google.com is blocked here; its file, CPU and date were not seen. fsehuf compresses faster than fpc 32 (574.79 versus 548.16 MB/s), so the win is decode speed. Last commit April 2022. The older owner name algorithm314/FPC (still linked from TurboBench's README) redirects to kagiannis/FPC.

notes: Every number in the record matches the README. tier_reason: The README table times one 1 MB file (RGC 0.01 s versus TurboRC rcc2senc() 0.03 s) with no CPU, no repeat count and no timing code; examples/rgc_demo.c only encodes, decodes and checks the round trip, it does not time anything or run TurboRC. The 2009 peer-reviewed paper (checked into the repo) shows about 2x faster encode and decode than a static arithmetic coder, but for a Delphi implementation against an unnamed in-house assembler AC, not this C library, so it does not lift the entry to B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'running about twice as fast as the simplest static 8-bit AC' and 'about twice as fast as a range coder' with moderate optimization. Table on tst.dat (1 MB): RGC 224,071 bytes in 0.01 s versus TurboRC rcc2senc() 237,380 bytes in 0.03 s (3x, derived from page data, at 0.01 s timer resolution); AC 8-bit 261,695 bytes with no time given. The 2009 paper (paper/recursive_group_coding_2009.pdf, Table 1, Calgary corpus average) reports 17.89 ms encode and 17.72 ms decode for RCGS versus 36.80 ms and 38.05 ms for a static assembler AC (about 2.1x, derived from page data), on a Delphi implementation.
corrections.caveats: The speed claim is mostly prose; the only timing table is a single 1 MB file with no CPU, no repeat count and no AC time, and the repo's rgc_demo.c contains no timing or TurboRC code, so the 0.01 s versus 0.03 s figures cannot be reproduced from the repo. Most of the table is compression ratio, not speed. The 2009 peer-reviewed paper (Telecommunications and Radio Engineering 68(20)) measured a Delphi implementation against an unnamed hand-written assembler AC with unstated hardware, not this C code. Author-run, so C.

notes: README numbers match the record. I opened the checked-in 2009 paper and added its Table 1 timings to claimed_speedup; it supports the 2x-versus-AC prose but not for this implementation.
